keyVerseText: And the coast of Manasseh was from Asher to Michmethah, that lieth before Shechem; and the border went along on the right hand unto the inhabitants of Entappuah.
rootMeaning: The term עֵין תַּפּוּחַ (ʻÊyn Tappûwach) combines two Hebrew words: עַיִן (ʻayin), meaning 'fountain' or 'spring,' and תַּפּוּחַ (tappûach), meaning 'apple.' This compound literally signifies 'fountain of the apple-tree,' evoking the image of a fresh water source associated with fruitful, life-giving trees. The root word עַיִן also carries connotations of sight, knowledge, and favor, enriching the literal sense beyond a mere place name to suggest a source of nourishment and blessing.
usageInScripture: This phrase appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Joshua 17:7, where it is translated as 'Entappuah.' The consistent use as a proper noun for a geographical location on the border between the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh indicates its primary function as a place name rather than a descriptive term. This singular occurrence underscores its significance as a boundary marker within the tribal allotments of Israel.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding עֵין תַּפּוּחַ as 'fountain of the apple-tree' invites reflection on God as the source of life and fruitfulness for His people. Just as a spring nourishes the land and sustains trees, so God provides spiritual nourishment and blessing to His covenant community. The imagery of an apple-tree, often associated with beauty and sustenance, points to the richness of God's provision and the flourishing found in His presence. Recognizing this place name's deeper meaning enriches our appreciation for the ways Scripture uses geography to symbolize divine care and the boundaries of His promises.
keyVerseReflection: Joshua 17:7 describes the border of Manasseh extending to the inhabitants of Entappuah, emphasizing the territorial limits assigned by God to His people. The mention of Entappuah as a boundary marker highlights the order and provision God established for Israel's inheritance. The name itself, 'fountain of the apple-tree,' subtly reminds readers that even the borders of God's people are marked by His sustaining grace and fruitful blessing.
